# Data Visualization

A chart is **read by people and executed by you**. This skill turns "make it look
good" into a procedure with checks, so the result is right by construction rather
than by taste.

**The method here is design-system-agnostic.** Nothing in the procedure, the form
heuristic, the six checks, or the mark specs is specific to one product. A design
system supplies a small set of *parameters* (its ramps, a categorical order, a
diverging pair, a status palette, a texture, its surfaces, its filter components);
the method consumes them unchanged. A **validated default palette** is the
reference instance, fully specified in `references/palette.md`. To target your
brand, read that file's structure and substitute its values - touch nothing else.

> The single most important habit: **the color part is computable, so compute it.**
> Never eyeball whether a palette is colorblind-safe - run `scripts/validate_palette.js`.

## The procedure - do these in order

Color comes LAST. Most bad charts pick colors first.

1. **Pick the form.** What is the data's job - magnitude, identity, polarity, a
   single headline, change-over-time? The job picks the chart type, and sometimes
   the answer is *not a chart* (a stat tile or hero number). -> `references/choosing-a-form.md`
2. **Assign color by the job it does.** Categorical (identity), sequential
   (magnitude), diverging (polarity), or status (state) - each has one rule.
   Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled. -> `references/color-formula.md`
3. **VALIDATE the palette - run the script, don't reason about Delta E.**
   `node scripts/validate_palette.js "<hex,hex,...>" --mode light` (relative to
   this skill's base directory - or load it as `<script type="module">` in the
   chart's own page, where it reads
   `data-palette` off `<body>` and logs a `console.table` report). It returns
   pass/fail on the lightness band, chroma floor, adjacent-pair CVD separation,
   the normal-vision floor, and contrast. Fix anything that FAILs before continuing. Re-run for
   `--mode dark` with that mode's surface.
4. **Apply mark specs & spacers.** Thin marks, 4px rounded data-ends anchored to
   the baseline, 2px lines, >=8px markers, a 2px surface gap between fills (stacked
   segments and adjacent bars alike) and a 2px surface ring on overlapping marks,
   selective direct labels. -> `references/marks-and-anatomy.md`
5. **Add the hover layer - by default.** An HTML/SVG chart *is* interactive; ship
   a crosshair+tooltip on line/area and a per-mark hover tooltip on bar/dot/cell.
   The only form that skips it is a bare stat tile with no plot. Hit targets bigger
   than the mark; filters in one row above the charts. -> `references/interaction.md`
6. **Final accessibility pass.** For >= 2 series a legend is always present and <= 4
   are also direct-labeled (a single series needs no legend box - the title names
   it), so identity is never color-alone; a table view exists; dark mode is **selected** - its own
   steps from the same ramps, validated against the dark surface, not an automatic
   flip; texture is available for the CVD/print/forced-colors case.
7. **Render it and look at it.** The validator checks color, not layout - open or
   screenshot the output and eyeball it for label collisions, geometry, and overflow
   before calling it done.

Then check the result against **`references/anti-patterns.md`** - it is the catalog
of what goes wrong. If your chart matches an entry, it's wrong.

## Non-negotiables (true in every design system)

- **Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled.** A 9th series is never a
  generated hue - it folds into "Other," small multiples, or composite encoding.
- **One axis.** Never a dual-axis chart (two y-scales). Two measures of different
  scale -> two charts, small multiples, or indexed to a common base. *(This is the
  #1 chart mistake - see anti-patterns.)*
- **Color follows the entity, never its rank.** A filter that changes the series
  count must not repaint the survivors.
- **Sequential = one hue, light->dark. Diverging = two hues + a neutral gray
  midpoint.** Never a rainbow; never a hue at the diverging midpoint.
- **Run the validator before shipping any categorical palette.** CVD Delta E >= 8 is the
  target (OKLab ×100); 6-8 is a floor that is legal ONLY with secondary encoding. A
  normal-vision floor below 15 is a hard FAIL - full-color readers can't tell the
  pair apart; re-step it on the adjacent pairlist (secondary encoding does not excuse
  this one); under `--pairs all` cut series or facet instead - see check 4. A contrast WARN
  obligates visible labels or a table view - it is not dismissable.
- **Thin marks; a legend always present for >= 2 series (none for one), with
  selective direct labels (never a number on every point); recessive grid/axes.**
- **Text wears text tokens, never the series color** - values, labels, and legends
  stay in primary/secondary/muted ink; a colored mark beside them carries identity.
- **Status colors are reserved** (good/warning/serious/critical) and never reused
  for "series 4"; they ship with an icon + label, never color alone.

## Plugging in a design system

The method is invariant; only these parameters change per system. The reference
instance - every value filled in - is `references/palette.md`.

| Parameter | What the system provides |
|---|---|
| **Ramps** | the hue scales (named steps) the palette draws from |
| **Categorical theme** | the fixed hue order (a named theme); default + alternates |
| **Sequential hue** | the default single hue for magnitude |
| **Diverging pair** | two warm/cool poles + a neutral midpoint |
| **Status palette** | good / warning / serious / critical - steps distinct from categorical |
| **Texture fill** | one directional hand-drawn fill, used at 45° / 135° |
| **Surfaces** | light & dark chart-surface colors (the validator needs these) |
| **Filter controls** | date-range & dimension controls (behavioral spec in `interaction.md`) |

To onboard a new system: fill those rows, feed its ramps to the validator, and let
it snap each slot to the nearest passing step. Structure and rules stay as written.

## Reference files

| File | What it answers |
|------|-----------------|
| `references/choosing-a-form.md` | Which chart type / is it even a chart? |
| `references/color-formula.md` | The four jobs, the six checks, snap-to-passing |
| `references/marks-and-anatomy.md` | Mark specs, spacers, labels, figures, hero number |
| `references/interaction.md` | Tooltips & hover, filters & time ranges |
| `references/components.md` | The pieces a chart is made of - build each in plain HTML |
| `references/anti-patterns.md` | **What goes wrong - check every chart against this** |
| `references/palette.md` | **The reference palette instance** - every parameter, filled in; swap for your brand's |
| `scripts/validate_palette.js` | Runnable six-checks validator (run it; don't eyeball) |

# Forecasting bake-off — Level 3 working directory

This directory is the working directory for the Level 3 prompt of a JRC C4
prompt-engineering demo. The full study description and the actual prompt
text live in `../../prompts/L3.md`.

## What you are doing

You are an AI agent invoked here to follow the prompt the operator has
pasted as the first user message. That prompt describes a six-model
univariate forecasting bake-off for German hourly electricity load on a
held-out 168-hour test window (2020-01-01 to 2020-01-07).

Stay inside this directory for all writes. Read freely from
`./opsd_de_load.csv`. Do not modify files outside this directory.

## Allowed and forbidden inputs

- **Allowed**: the load series; features derivable from the `utc_timestamp`
  column (hour, day-of-week, month, is_weekend, German public holidays via
  the `holidays` package); lag features and rolling-window features from
  the load itself.
- **Forbidden (external data)**: temperature, weather, gas prices, market
  prices, anything not in `opsd_de_load.csv`.

Time-derived features and German public holidays are *not* exogenous in the
forecasting sense — they are knowable a priori without consulting any other
dataset, so they are allowed.

## Output structure (you write into the current directory)

```
code/
    common.py
    naive.py
    sarima.py
    prophet.py
    lightgbm_features.py
    nbeats.py
    patchtst.py
    forecast.py            — orchestrator
figures/
    01_overview.png        — full series + test window highlighted
    02_forecast_comparison.png  — 2 × 3 small-multiples grid
    03_metric_comparison.png    — MAPE / RMSE / MAE bars
    04_per_day_mape.png         — per-day MAPE per model
    05_winner_with_intervals.png— winner with 80/95% PI bands
    06_residuals.png             — winner residuals by hour and day
    07_feature_importance.png    — only if LightGBM is in top 2
    08_decomposition.png         — only if Prophet is in top 2
metrics.json
metrics.csv
transcript.md
```

All figures: 300 dpi, sans-serif, units in axis labels, non-overlapping
legends, consistent qualitative palette across all panels so each model
keeps its colour throughout.

## `metrics.json` schema

```json
{
  "test_start": "2020-01-01",
  "test_end":   "2020-01-07",
  "n_test_observations": 168,
  "models": [
    {
      "name": "<naive|sarima|prophet|lightgbm|nbeats|patchtst>",
      "mape_test_pct": 0.0,
      "rmse_test_mw":  0.0,
      "mae_test_mw":   0.0,
      "mape_jan1_pct": 0.0,
      "mape_jan2_to_jan7_pct": 0.0,
      "runtime_seconds": 0.0,
      "hyperparameters": {}
    }
  ],
  "winner": "<model name>",
  "winner_coverage_80pct": 0.0,
  "winner_coverage_95pct": 0.0,
  "winner_pinball_loss_q10": 0.0,
  "winner_pinball_loss_q50": 0.0,
  "winner_pinball_loss_q90": 0.0,
  "total_runtime_seconds": 0.0
}
```

## Do NOT

- Do not write outside this directory.
- Do not pull in external data sources (weather, prices, etc.).
- Do not use the test window (2020-01-01 to 2020-01-07) for any model
  fitting, hyperparameter selection, or model-class choice.
- Do not skip the refit-on-Train+Validation step before forecasting test.
- Do not silently drop or impute missing hours (the data is clean — verify).
- Do not install additional Python packages. The venv at `../../.venv` has
  everything: `pandas`, `numpy`, `matplotlib`, `statsmodels`, `pmdarima`,
  `darts[all]` (which bundles Prophet, torch, xgboost, etc.), `lightgbm`,
  and `holidays`. If your shell's `python` resolves elsewhere, use
  `../../.venv/bin/python` directly.
- Do not commit to git from inside your run. The human operator commits
  the directory after the run completes.

## Style

- All code comments and `transcript.md` prose: plain language, Feynman-
  style. The audience is JRC policy economists and engineers, not ML
  researchers. Avoid jargon you would not unpack.
- No emoji in code, comments, or transcripts.
- Type hints on every function signature.
- One module per model (see `code/` layout above), with a thin orchestrator
  (`code/forecast.py`) that imports them and writes the outputs.

1	# Anti-patterns - what goes wrong
2	
3	Check every chart against this list. If your output matches an entry, it is wrong -
4	fix it before shipping. These are real failure modes, each caught in shipping
5	dashboards.
6	
7	## Color & encoding
8	
9	**Bad: Dual-axis charts (two y-scales on one plot).**
10	Why it misleads: the alignment of the two scales is arbitrary, so the chart invents a
11	correlation that isn't in the data. Real example: an "Adoption" chart plotting Users
12	(0-30k) against Sessions (0-800k) - a reviewer flagged it as looking "hallucinated."
13	Good: Do instead: two charts, small multiples, or index both series to a common base
14	(=100 at t0) on **one** axis.
15	
16	**Bad: Recolor-on-filter.** Assigning colors by current rank, so filtering out a series
17	repaints the survivors.
18	Why: a reader who learned "Acme is blue" is now misled.
19	Good: Color follows the entity, not its row number. Survivors keep their hue.
20	
21	**Bad: Cycling / generating hues past 8.** A 9th categorical color, generated or reused.
22	Why: indistinguishable from an existing slot under CVD; breaks the order check.
23	Good: Fold the tail into "Other," facet into small multiples, or use composite encoding.
24	
25	**Bad: Eyeballing colorblind-safety.** "These look different enough."
26	Good: Run `scripts/validate_palette.js`. Adjacent Delta E >= 8 (OKLab ×100), or 6-8 WITH secondary encoding.
27	
28	**Bad: A value-ramp on nominal categories.** Coloring each bar darker-where-bigger
29	when the categories have no natural order (products, teams, endpoints).
30	Why: it double-encodes bar length as hue, burns the only free channel on
31	information the chart already shows, and fails the categorical checks by design
32	(a ramp spans the lightness band and drops below the chroma floor).
33	Good: One series -> one color (slot 1) for every bar. Ordered categories (funnel,
34	tiers, age bands) -> the ordinal ramp, validated with `--ordinal`.
35	
36	**Bad: Rainbow / non-neighbor sequential.** A multi-hue ramp for magnitude.
37	Good: One hue, light->dark. (Analogous neighbors or semantic heat are the only multi-hue
38	sequential exceptions, always with a scale legend.)
39	
40	**Bad: A hue at the diverging midpoint, or two cool hues as the two poles.**
41	Why: the midpoint must read as "nothing"; poles must read as opposite. blue<->aqua
42	fails this (both cool); blue<->red or blue<->orange succeed (warm/cool).
43	Good: Two hues that read as opposite + a neutral gray midpoint.
44	
45	**Bad: Status color used for a non-status series** (or a series color used for status).
46	Good: Status tokens only when the color *means* good/bad; categorical when it's identity.
47	
48	## Form
49	
50	**Bad: Eight categorical hues when the story is one number.** The most common way a
51	chart misses its point.
52	Good: Emphasis (highlight one, gray the rest), or a stat tile / hero number.
53	
54	**Bad: A one-bar bar chart, or a 2-slice pie.**
55	Good: A stat tile. The number is the chart.
56	
57	**Bad: A donut/pie for comparing close values.**
58	Good: A bar, or the numbers. Part-to-whole at a glance only, <= 6 segments.
59	
60	**Bad: More than ~7 color classes carrying meaning.**
61	Good: A table, or table + chart. Past ~7 bins, adjacent classes blur.
62	
63	## Marks & chrome
64	
65	**Bad: Thick saturated blocks, heavy gridlines, no breathing room.** Reads loud, even
66	childish, at scale.
67	Good: Thin marks, hairline recessive grid/axes, generous padding. Saturated fills are
68	for small marks and accents, never large blocks.
69	
70	**Bad: Dashed gridlines or axis rules.** Dashing adds visual noise and reads as
71	"projection" or "threshold" when it's just a grid.
72	Good: Gridlines and axes are solid hairlines, one shade off the surface.
73	
74	**Bad: A number on every data point.** A value beside every dot or segment is chaos and goes unread.
75	Good: A legend is always present for >= 2 series; direct-label *selectively* (the endpoint, the extreme, the one series that matters) and let the axis + tooltip carry the rest.
76	
77	**Bad: A border drawn around marks to separate them.**
78	Good: A 2px surface gap between fills (stacked segments and adjacent bars alike) and a 2px surface ring (on overlapping markers).
79	
80	**Bad: A label clipped by, or overflowing, a too-small bar or stacked segment** -
81	including `overflow: hidden` cropping the first/last characters of an in-segment label.
82	Good: Only render a label inside a mark when it fits with padding; otherwise move it
83	outside the bar end, or drop it to the tooltip/legend (the value stays in the table view).
84	
85	**Bad: A chart container whose fixed height excludes the x-axis band** - the plot
86	fits, the axis labels don't, so the card gets a tiny nested vertical scroll.
87	Good: Size the container to include the axis labels (plot height + x-axis band),
88	or let the container grow with its content instead of fixing a height.
89	
90	**Bad: A display or serif face on the hero figure.** It reads as off-brand decoration.
91	Good: The hero figure uses the same sans as everything else.
92	
93	**Bad: `tabular-nums` on a large standalone number.** Equal-width digits make `121`
94	look loose at display sizes.
95	Good: Proportional figures on hero and stat-tile values; `tabular-nums` only where
96	numbers align vertically (table rows, axis ticks).
97	
98	**Bad: Texture on by default, or as decoration.** Dense angled fields are a vestibular
99	risk and read as noise on value scales.
100	Good: Texture is opt-in (a11y setting, print, forced-colors), 45°/135° only, ordered on
101	value scales.
102	
103	## Interaction & accessibility
104	
105	**Bad: A tooltip as the only way to read a value.**
106	Good: Tooltips enhance, never gate - every value is also reachable via direct labels or
107	the table view; keyboard focus shows the same as hover.
108	
109	**Bad: Pinpoint hover targets - an 8px scatter dot you must land on dead-center.**
110	Good: The hit area includes the 2px gap and meets a ~24px minimum; dense scatter uses a nearest-point / Voronoi layer.
111	
112	**Bad: Per-chart filters, or filters inside a chart card.**
113	Good: One filter row above everything it scopes; all charts re-render against the same slice.
114	
115	**Bad: Skeleton flash on refetch.**
116	Good: Hold the previous render at reduced opacity - no layout jump.
117	
118	**Bad: No table view / color-only encoding on a continuous scale.**
119	Good: Every chart has a table-view twin (the WCAG-clean equivalent).
120

repaints the survivors.
Why: a reader who learned "Acme is blue" is now misled.
Good: Color follows the entity, not its row number. Survivors keep their hue.

**Bad: Cycling / generating hues past 8.** A 9th categorical color, generated or reused.
Why: indistinguishable from an existing slot under CVD; breaks the order check.
Good: Fold the tail into "Other," facet into small multiples, or use composite encoding.

**Bad: Eyeballing colorblind-safety.** "These look different enough."
Good: Run `scripts/validate_palette.js`. Adjacent Delta E >= 8 (OKLab ×100), or 6-8 WITH secondary encoding.

**Bad: A value-ramp on nominal categories.** Coloring each bar darker-where-bigger
when the categories have no natural order (products, teams, endpoints).
Why: it double-encodes bar length as hue, burns the only free channel on
information the chart already shows, and fails the categorical checks by design
(a ramp spans the lightness band and drops below the chroma floor).
Good: One series -> one color (slot 1) for every bar. Ordered categories (funnel,
tiers, age bands) -> the ordinal ramp, validated with `--ordinal`.

**Bad: Rainbow / non-neighbor sequential.** A multi-hue ramp for magnitude.
Good: One hue, light->dark. (Analogous neighbors or semantic heat are the only multi-hue
sequential exceptions, always with a scale legend.)

**Bad: A hue at the diverging midpoint, or two cool hues as the two poles.**
Why: the midpoint must read as "nothing"; poles must read as opposite. blue<->aqua
fails this (both cool); blue<->red or blue<->orange succeed (warm/cool).
Good: Two hues that read as opposite + a neutral gray midpoint.

**Bad: Status color used for a non-status series** (or a series color used for status).
Good: Status tokens only when the color *means* good/bad; categorical when it's identity.

## Form

**Bad: Eight categorical hues when the story is one number.** The most common way a
chart misses its point.
Good: Emphasis (highlight one, gray the rest), or a stat tile / hero number.

**Bad: A one-bar bar chart, or a 2-slice pie.**
Good: A stat tile. The number is the chart.

**Bad: A donut/pie for comparing close values.**
Good: A bar, or the numbers. Part-to-whole at a glance only, <= 6 segments.

**Bad: More than ~7 color classes carrying meaning.**
Good: A table, or table + chart. Past ~7 bins, adjacent classes blur.

## Marks & chrome

**Bad: Thick saturated blocks, heavy gridlines, no breathing room.** Reads loud, even
childish, at scale.
Good: Thin marks, hairline recessive grid/axes, generous padding. Saturated fills are
for small marks and accents, never large blocks.

**Bad: Dashed gridlines or axis rules.** Dashing adds visual noise and reads as
"projection" or "threshold" when it's just a grid.
Good: Gridlines and axes are solid hairlines, one shade off the surface.

**Bad: A number on every data point.** A value beside every dot or segment is chaos and goes unread.
Good: A legend is always present for >= 2 series; direct-label *selectively* (the endpoint, the extreme, the one series that matters) and let the axis + tooltip carry the rest.

**Bad: A border drawn around marks to separate them.**
Good: A 2px surface gap between fills (stacked segments and adjacent bars alike) and a 2px surface ring (on overlapping markers).

**Bad: A label clipped by, or overflowing, a too-small bar or stacked segment** -
including `overflow: hidden` cropping the first/last characters of an in-segment label.
Good: Only render a label inside a mark when it fits with padding; otherwise move it
outside the bar end, or drop it to the tooltip/legend (the value stays in the table view).

**Bad: A chart container whose fixed height excludes the x-axis band** - the plot
fits, the axis labels don't, so the card gets a tiny nested vertical scroll.
Good: Size the container to include the axis labels (plot height + x-axis band),
or let the container grow with its content instead of fixing a height.

**Bad: A display or serif face on the hero figure.** It reads as off-brand decoration.
Good: The hero figure uses the same sans as everything else.

**Bad: `tabular-nums` on a large standalone number.** Equal-width digits make `121`
look loose at display sizes.
Good: Proportional figures on hero and stat-tile values; `tabular-nums` only where
numbers align vertically (table rows, axis ticks).

**Bad: Texture on by default, or as decoration.** Dense angled fields are a vestibular
risk and read as noise on value scales.
Good: Texture is opt-in (a11y setting, print, forced-colors), 45°/135° only, ordered on
value scales.

## Interaction & accessibility

**Bad: A tooltip as the only way to read a value.**
Good: Tooltips enhance, never gate - every value is also reachable via direct labels or
the table view; keyboard focus shows the same as hover.

**Bad: Pinpoint hover targets - an 8px scatter dot you must land on dead-center.**
Good: The hit area includes the 2px gap and meets a ~24px minimum; dense scatter uses a nearest-point / Voronoi layer.

**Bad: Per-chart filters, or filters inside a chart card.**
Good: One filter row above everything it scopes; all charts re-render against the same slice.

**Bad: Skeleton flash on refetch.**
Good: Hold the previous render at reduced opacity - no layout jump.

**Bad: No table view / color-only encoding on a continuous scale.**
Good: Every chart has a table-view twin (the WCAG-clean equivalent).

Every categorical color - current or proposed - must pass all six.

1. **Fixed hue anchors.** Eight families in a fixed order. The order is the

input.content:
# Frozen study plan

1. Verify the CSV without modifying it; assert 50,400 positive hourly values, UTC continuity, exact endpoints and train/validation/test counts. `code/common.py` owns loading, split boundaries, metrics and forecast result records. Only the overview may read post-test observations.
2. All six models predict 168 hours from one origin without test observations. Validate using consecutive non-overlapping origins starting 2019-10-01, every 168 hours, including the final 24-hour remainder. Parameters are fit on training data only; previous validation observations may supply context for later validation forecasts, never gradients or coefficient fitting. Score the concatenated 2,208 validation hours with MAPE. Refit every selected configuration from scratch on training plus validation.
3. `code/naive.py` repeats the last observed week. `code/sarima.py` compares two explicit daily SARIMAX orders, with deterministic weekly Fourier regressors derived from timestamps to represent weekly structure honestly. `code/prophet.py` uses Darts Prophet with federal German holidays and daily, weekly and yearly seasonality, comparing two changepoint priors.
4. `code/lightgbm_features.py` compares two tree complexities with prescribed calendar, lag and strictly past rolling features. Recursively substitute predictions for all unobserved lag/rolling values within each week. Fit five quantile models (0.025, 0.1, 0.5, 0.9, 0.975) under the selected configuration for both 80% and 95% intervals; explicitly label recursive intervals as approximate marginal intervals.
5. `code/nbeats.py` preserves the default stack configuration with smaller layer width for a CPU budget. `code/patchtst.py` uses actual PatchTST if present, otherwise Darts TransformerModel, not a mislabeled MLP mixer. Both use 168-hour input/output, quantile likelihood, training-only scaling, up to 30 epochs, and early stopping on the identical rolling-origin validation MAPE. Select epoch count, then refit from scratch for that many epochs. Stride-168 training examples cover the training history without expensive hourly near-duplicates. No tuning uses test scores.
6. `code/forecast.py` orchestrates all six and saves their forecasts and validation records before test scoring. `code/figures.py` produces the required labeled 300-dpi figures. Grouped metric bars use ratios to the baseline with labels showing raw % or MW, avoiding mixed-unit axes. Optional diagnostics depend only on the requested top-two rule. `transcript.md` is a short methods and results report with model limitations, uncertainty diagnostics and reproduction instructions.
7. Verify metric formulas, recursive non-leakage, time splits and quantile ordering with executable tests in `code/test_study.py`. Run the full study, independently recompute metrics from saved predictions, visually inspect figures and inventory every required output. No package installations, external covariates, git operations or writes outside this directory.

Assumptions: UTC calendar days define metrics and timestamp features, with federal holidays only. Jan 2-7 means non-Jan-1 days, not exclusively working days (it includes a weekend). The seasonal-naive baseline may legitimately win; in that event no native interval coverage is fabricated. The task's illustrative annual-lag timestamp is incorrect: 2020-01-01 00:00 UTC minus 8760 hours is 2019-01-01 00:00 UTC. The six classes are fixed before test evaluation; calling the lowest test-MAPE model the winner does not justify production selection on that week alone.

1	# Forecasting bake-off — Level 3 working directory
2	
3	This directory is the working directory for the Level 3 prompt of a JRC C4
4	prompt-engineering demo. The full study description and the actual prompt
5	text live in `../../prompts/L3.md`.
6	
7	## What you are doing
8	
9	You are an AI agent invoked here to follow the prompt the operator has
10	pasted as the first user message. That prompt describes a six-model
11	univariate forecasting bake-off for German hourly electricity load on a
12	held-out 168-hour test window (2020-01-01 to 2020-01-07).
13	
14	Stay inside this directory for all writes. Read freely from
15	`./opsd_de_load.csv`. Do not modify files outside this directory.
16	
17	## Allowed and forbidden inputs
18	
19	- **Allowed**: the load series; features derivable from the `utc_timestamp`
20	  column (hour, day-of-week, month, is_weekend, German public holidays via
21	  the `holidays` package); lag features and rolling-window features from
22	  the load itself.
23	- **Forbidden (external data)**: temperature, weather, gas prices, market
24	  prices, anything not in `opsd_de_load.csv`.
25	
26	Time-derived features and German public holidays are *not* exogenous in the
27	forecasting sense — they are knowable a priori without consulting any other
28	dataset, so they are allowed.
29	
30	## Output structure (you write into the current directory)
31	
32	```
33	code/
34	    common.py
35	    naive.py
36	    sarima.py
37	    prophet.py
38	    lightgbm_features.py
39	    nbeats.py
40	    patchtst.py
41	    forecast.py            — orchestrator
42	figures/
43	    01_overview.png        — full series + test window highlighted
44	    02_forecast_comparison.png  — 2 × 3 small-multiples grid
45	    03_metric_comparison.png    — MAPE / RMSE / MAE bars
46	    04_per_day_mape.png         — per-day MAPE per model
47	    05_winner_with_intervals.png— winner with 80/95% PI bands
48	    06_residuals.png             — winner residuals by hour and day
49	    07_feature_importance.png    — only if LightGBM is in top 2
50	    08_decomposition.png         — only if Prophet is in top 2
51	metrics.json
52	metrics.csv
53	transcript.md
54	```
55	
56	All figures: 300 dpi, sans-serif, units in axis labels, non-overlapping
57	legends, consistent qualitative palette across all panels so each model
58	keeps its colour throughout.
59	
60	## `metrics.json` schema
61	
62	```json
63	{

86	}

92	- Do not pull in external data sources (weather, prices, etc.).

        """
        The "likelihood" corresponding to quantile regression.
        It uses the Quantile Loss Metric for custom quantiles centered around q=0.5.

        This class can be used as any other Likelihood objects even though it is not

        Parameters
        ----------
        quantiles

        """
        if quantiles is None:
            self.quantiles = [
                0.01,
                0.05,
                0.1,
                0.15,
                0.2,
                0.25,
                0.3,
                0.4,
                0.5,
                0.6,
                0.7,
                0.75,
                0.8,
                0.85,
                0.9,
                0.95,
                0.99,
            ]
        else:
            self.quantiles = sorted(quantiles)
        _check_quantiles(self.quantiles)
        self._median_idx = self.quantiles.index(0.5)
        self.first = True
        self.quantiles_tensor = None

        super().__init__(
            likelihood_type=LikelihoodType.Quantile,
            parameter_names=quantile_names(self.quantiles),
            prior_strength=1.0,
        )
        # ignore additional attributes
        self.ignore_attrs_equality += ["_median_idx", "first", "quantiles_tensor"]

    def sample(self, model_output: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        """
        Sample uniformly between [0, 1] (for each batch example) and return the linear interpolation between the fitted
        quantiles closest to the sampled value.

        model_output is of shape (batch_size, n_timesteps, n_components, n_quantiles)

        device = model_output.device
        num_samples, n_timesteps, n_components, n_quantiles = model_output.shape

                num_samples,

            )

        # add dummy dim
        probas = probs.unsqueeze(-2)

        # tile and transpose
        p = torch.tile(probas, (1, 1, 1, n_quantiles, 1)).transpose(4, 3)

        # prepare quantiles
        tquantiles = torch.tensor(self.quantiles).reshape((1, 1, 1, -1)).to(device)

        # calculate index of biggest quantile smaller than the sampled value
        left_idx = torch.sum(p > tquantiles, dim=-1)

        # obtain index of smallest quantile bigger than sampled value
        right_idx = left_idx + 1

        # repeat the model output on the edges
        repeat_count = [1] * n_quantiles
        repeat_count[0] = 2
        repeat_count[-1] = 2
        repeat_count = torch.tensor(repeat_count).to(device)
        shifted_output = torch.repeat_interleave(model_output, repeat_count, dim=-1)

        # obtain model output values corresponding to the quantiles left and right of the sampled value
        left_value = torch.gather(shifted_output, index=left_idx, dim=-1)
        right_value = torch.gather(shifted_output, index=right_idx, dim=-1)

        # add 0 and 1 to quantiles
        ext_quantiles = [0.0] + self.quantiles + [1.0]
        expanded_q = torch.tile(torch.tensor(ext_quantiles), left_idx.shape).to(device)

        # calculate closest quantiles to the sampled value
        left_q = torch.gather(expanded_q, index=left_idx, dim=-1)
        right_q = torch.gather(expanded_q, index=right_idx, dim=-1)

        # linear interpolation
        weights = (probs - left_q) / (right_q - left_q)
        inter = left_value + weights * (right_value - left_value)

        parameters must be extracted differently."""

        params = model_output.reshape(
            num_samples, n_timesteps, n_components * n_quantiles
        )
        return params

    def compute_loss(
        self,
        model_output: torch.Tensor,
        target: torch.Tensor,
        sample_weight: torch.Tensor,
    ):
        """
        We are re-defining a custom loss (which is not a likelihood loss) compared to Likelihood

        Parameters
        ----------
        model_output
            must be of shape (batch_size, n_timesteps, n_target_variables, n_quantiles)
        target
            must be of shape (n_samples, n_timesteps, n_target_variables)
        sample_weight
            must be of shape (n_samples, n_timesteps, n_target_variables)
        """
        dim_q = 3
        device = model_output.device

        # test if torch model forward produces correct output and store quantiles tensor
        if self.first:

                len(model_output.shape) == 4
                and len(target.shape) == 3
                and model_output.shape[:2] == target.shape[:2],
                "mismatch between predicted and target shape",
            )
            raise_if_not(
                model_output.shape[dim_q] == len(self.quantiles),
                "mismatch between number of predicted quantiles and target quantiles",
            )
            self.quantiles_tensor = torch.tensor(self.quantiles).to(device)
            self.first = False

        errors = target.unsqueeze(-1) - model_output
        losses = torch.max(
            (self.quantiles_tensor - 1) * errors, self.quantiles_tensor * errors
        ).sum(dim=dim_q)

        if sample_weight is not None:
            losses = losses * sample_weight
        return losses.mean()

        return None

    def _predict(
        self,

        num_samples: int = 1,

    ) -> TimeSeries:
        _ = self._check_seasonality_conditions(future_covariates=future_covariates)

            )

        return self._build_forecast_series(forecast)

    def _add_capacities_to_df(self, df: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
        dates = df["ds"]
        try:
            df["cap"] = self._cap(dates) if callable(self._cap) else self._cap
            df["floor"] = self._floor(dates) if callable(self._floor) else self._floor
        except ValueError as e:
            raise_if(
                "does not match length of index" in str(e),
                "Callables supplied to `Prophet.set_capacity` as `cap` or `floor` "
                "arguments have to return Sequences of identical length as their "
                " input argument Sequence!",
                logger,
            )
            raise
        return df

    def _generate_predict_df(
        self, n: int, future_covariates: Optional[TimeSeries] = None
    ) -> pd.DataFrame:
        """Returns a pandas DataFrame in the format required for Prophet.predict() with `n` dates after the end of
        the fitted TimeSeries"""

        predict_df = pd.DataFrame(data={"ds": self._generate_new_dates(n)})
        if self.is_logistic:
            predict_df = self._add_capacities_to_df(predict_df)
        if future_covariates is not None:
            predict_df = predict_df.merge(
                future_covariates.to_dataframe(),
                left_on="ds",
                right_index=True,
                how="left",
            )
        return predict_df

    def _check_seasonality_conditions(
        self, future_covariates: Optional[TimeSeries] = None
    ) -> list[str]:
        """
        Checks if the conditions for custom conditional seasonalities are met. Each custom seasonality that has a
        `condition_name` other than None is checked. If the `condition_name` is not a column in the `future_covariates`
        or if the values in the column are not all True or False, an error is raised.
        Returns a list of the `condition_name`s of the conditional seasonalities that have been checked.

        Parameters
        ----------
        future_covariates
            optionally, a TimeSeries containing the future covariates and including the columns that are used as
            conditions for the conditional seasonalities when necessary

        Raises
        ------
        ValueError
            if a seasonality has a `condition_name` and a column named `condition_name` is missing in
            the `future_covariates`

            if a seasonality has a `condition_name` and the values in the corresponding column in `future_covariates`
            are not binary values (True or False, 1 or 0)
        """

        conditional_seasonality_covariates = []
        invalid_conditional_seasonalities = []
        if future_covariates is not None:
            future_covariates_columns = future_covariates.columns
        else:
            future_covariates_columns = []

        for seasonality_name, attributes in self._add_seasonalities.items():
            condition_name = attributes["condition_name"]
            if condition_name is not None:
                if condition_name not in future_covariates_columns:
                    invalid_conditional_seasonalities.append((
                        seasonality_name,
                        condition_name,
                        "column missing",
                    ))
                    continue
                if (
                    not future_covariates[condition_name]
                    .to_series()
                    .isin([True, False])
                    .all()
                ):
                    invalid_conditional_seasonalities.append((
                        seasonality_name,
                        condition_name,
                        "invalid values",
                    ))
                    continue
                conditional_seasonality_covariates.append(condition_name)

        if len(invalid_conditional_seasonalities) > 0:
            formatted_issues_str = ", ".join(
                f"'{name}' (condition_name: '{cond}'; issue: {reason})"
                for name, cond, reason in invalid_conditional_seasonalities
            )
            raise_log(
                ValueError(
                    f"The following seasonalities have invalid conditions: {formatted_issues_str}. "
                    f"Each conditional seasonality must be accompanied by a binary component/column in the "
                    f"`future_covariates` with the same name as the `condition_name`"
                ),
                logger,
            )
        return conditional_seasonality_covariates

        return False

    @property
    def supports_probabilistic_prediction(self) -> bool:
        return True

    def _stochastic_samples(self, predict_df, n_samples) -> np.ndarray:
        """Returns stochastic forecast of `n_samples` samples.
        This method is a replicate of Prophet.predict() which suspends simplification of stochastic samples to
        deterministic target values."""

        self.model.uncertainty_samples = n_samples

    def _create_transformer_inputs(self, data):
        # '_TimeSeriesSequentialDataset' stores time series in the
        # (batch_size, input_chunk_length, input_size) format. PyTorch's nn.Transformer
        # module needs it the (input_chunk_length, batch_size, input_size) format.
        # Therefore, the first two dimensions need to be swapped.
        src = data.permute(1, 0, 2)
        tgt = src[-1:, :, :]

        return src, tgt

    @io_processor
    def forward(self, x_in: PLModuleInput):
        data, _, _ = x_in
        # Here we create 'src' and 'tgt', the inputs for the encoder and decoder
        # side of the Transformer architecture
        src, tgt = self._create_transformer_inputs(data)

        # "math.sqrt(self.input_size)" is a normalization factor
        # see section 3.2.1 in 'Attention is All you Need' by Vaswani et al. (2017)
        src = self.encoder(src) * math.sqrt(self.input_size)
        src = self.positional_encoding(src)

        tgt = self.encoder(tgt) * math.sqrt(self.input_size)
        tgt = self.positional_encoding(tgt)

        x = self.transformer(src=src, tgt=tgt)
        out = self.decoder(x)

        # Here we change the data format
        # from (1, batch_size, output_chunk_length * output_size)
        # to (batch_size, output_chunk_length, output_size, nr_params)
        predictions = out[0, :, :]
        predictions = predictions.view(
            -1, self.target_length, self.target_size, self.nr_params
        )

        return predictions

Actually, I realize stride-168 training is genuinely problematic: with 41616 training hours minus 336 lookback, only ~245 non-overlapping windows exist per epoch, meaning 30 epochs gives just 7350 gradient examples total — badly data-starved for NBEATS' default capacity. Worse, since 2015-01-01 is a Thursday, every window with stride 168 starts at exactly Thursday 00:00, so the model never learns from inputs beginning on other weekdays — a real methodological flaw, not just an efficiency issue.

Actually since Darts builds windows backwards from the training end by default, the anchoring still locks in a single weekday phase regardless of stride direction. Without covariates encoding weekday/hour, NBEATS has no explicit signal for phase and can only infer it implicitly from the 168-hour pattern itself, so I should recommend adding datetime attribute encoders (allowed per AGENTS.md) alongside a shorter stride to expose more phase diversity.

Compute-wise, NBEATS with ~1715 samples over 30 epochs on CPU is fine, and the default Transformer config should also run quickly. For rolling validation across 14 origins, each prediction call over the full history is manageable, though the final remainder origin only covers 24 hours, so I'll score just that partial horizon and note it creates a slightly different horizon distribution than the test set — a minor asymmetry.

For SARIMAX, tractability is the real concern: with seasonal period 24 on 41,616 observations, the state-space dimension and Kalman filter cost per likelihood evaluation could make L-BFGS optimization take tens of minutes per fit, and I'd need four such fits total. That's feasible but risky, so I'm considering constraining the fit window (e.g., last two years) to keep runtime reasonable, though that shifts away from strictly "fit on full training only."

I should also handle rolling forecasts by refitting parameters and using `apply`/`append` to extend the fitted results with new observations before calling `get_forecast`. But a real gap in the plan: it only accounts for weekly Fourier terms, not annual seasonality or holidays -- and since the test week includes New Year's Day, the SARIMA model has no way to capture that anomaly. I'd want to add a holiday dummy variable to account for this.

I'm also thinking through whether Darts' Prophet wrapper supports built-in holiday effects via its country_holidays parameter, which would be a cleaner solution there. And for coverage/interval reporting, if the naive baseline wins but has no native prediction intervals, I should generate legitimate empirical intervals from validation residuals rather than leaving those fields null or fabricating numbers -- a conformal-style approach using per-horizon quantiles of past errors, paired with pinball loss at the 10th, 50th, and 90th percentiles.

For the quantile models, I'm noting that Darts' default quantile set doesn't include 0.025/0.975, so a 95% interval wouldn't actually be available unless I explicitly specify those quantiles for NBEATS. I also need to watch out for quantile crossing in LightGBM's quantile regression (unlike Darts' QuantileRegression, which samples and is naturally ordered) -- the fix is to sort quantiles per timestamp during post-processing and document that step.

For recursive forecasting, lag features under 168 hours end up using predicted values rather than observations, so rolling features built on those predictions will accumulate error over the horizon; this is an accepted tradeoff since the plan calls for recursive rather than direct multi-horizon modeling, and the quantile models riding along on the same recursive median-driven features only give approximate marginal intervals. MAPE's definition checks out cleanly for the Jan-1 comparison, and early stopping should use rolling MAPE evaluated each epoch across a 30-epoch budget to pick the right stopping point.

I also need to confirm the scaler is fit only on training data initially, then refit on train+validation for the final model — consistent and leak-free. Validation isn't perfectly fair across models since SARIMAX, Naive, LightGBM, and N-BEATS all use context windows while Prophet can't, so that asymmetry should just be documented rather than fixed. Refitting SARIMAX from scratch on the combined train+validation set means re-estimating on all 43,824 observations, which is another lengthy fit, but I can limit this to just the selected configuration rather than refitting everything. Checking for leakage elsewhere: deep model scaling uses training data only, LightGBM has no scaling, Fourier terms come from timestamps, and holidays are known a priori — all clean.

Verifying the positive hourly values count checks out at 50,400 with a minimum above 31,000. The test split math works out too: starting October 1st 2019 with non-overlapping 168-hour origins gives exactly 13 full weeks plus a final 24-hour window ending December 31st, which matches the plan.

For reproducibility, I need to force the accelerator to CPU explicitly in the trainer kwargs, since Darts defaults to "auto" and would otherwise select MPS on this Mac, which has known determinism issues. Also noting that PatchTST isn't available in Darts 0.41, so the fallback TransformerModel — a standard encoder-decoder transformer — needs to be labeled accurately in the metrics output.

I should still name it "patchtst" per the schema while disclosing the substitution in the transcript. The Darts TransformerModel with QuantileRegression likelihood should work fine for one-shot 168-hour output prediction. I want to double-check the Darts 0.41 API details—fit stride parameter, checkpoint loading, QuantileRegression defaults, NBEATS defaults, add_encoders—and review L3.md, plus consider benchmarking the SARIMAX daily order fitting speed with statsmodels.

A quick full benchmark would eat minutes, so instead I'll time SARIMAX fitting with order (1,0,1)(1,1,1,24) on a smaller sample of 8760 points and extrapolate from there, running it with a timeout in the background.

1	# TASK
2	
3	You are running a small, reproducible **forecasting bake-off** for German
4	national hourly electricity load. Treat this exercise like a short methods
5	section of a peer-reviewed paper: multiple model classes are fit on the same
6	data, evaluated on the same held-out test window, and compared on the same
7	metrics. Produce publication-grade figures, a transparent metrics table, and
8	a written discussion of which model wins and where each one fails.
9	
10	The deliverable is a self-contained study an external reviewer could read in
11	under five minutes and reproduce in under thirty.
12	
13	# BACKGROUND
14	
15	## Data
16	
17	- File: `opsd_de_load.csv` (in the current working directory). Columns:
18	    - `utc_timestamp` — ISO-8601, hourly, UTC
19	    - `DE_load_actual_entsoe_transparency` — load in megawatts
20	- Coverage: 2015-01-01 00:00 UTC to 2020-09-30 23:00 UTC, hourly,
21	  exactly 50,400 rows, no NaN, no gaps.
22	- Source: Open Power System Data, derived from ENTSO-E Transparency Platform.
23	
24	## Models to compare
25	
26	Compare **all six** of the following, end-to-end. The point of this exercise
27	is the bake-off, not picking a favourite a priori.
28	
29	1. **Seasonal-naive baseline** — the forecast for hour *t* is the observed
30	   load at hour *t* − 168 h (same hour, one week earlier). Anchor for
31	   relative comparisons; everything else should beat this.
32	
33	2. **SARIMA** — classical statistical approach. Fit via
34	   `pmdarima.auto_arima` with weekly seasonality (m=168 is impractical;
35	   use m=24 daily seasonality and let weekly structure emerge from
36	   differencing) **or** via `statsmodels` SARIMAX with explicit
37	   `(p,d,q)(P,D,Q,s)` orders chosen by the validation MAPE.
38	
39	3. **Prophet with German holidays** — via `darts.models.Prophet`. Use
40	   `country_holidays="DE"` (or pass holidays explicitly via the
41	   `holidays.Germany()` package). Daily + weekly + yearly seasonality.
42	
43	4. **LightGBM on engineered features** — via `lightgbm.LGBMRegressor`
44	   directly (cleaner than darts wrapper for feature work). Features:
45	     - Time index: `hour`, `day_of_week`, `month`, `is_weekend`,
46	       `is_public_holiday_de` (use `holidays.Germany()` for the indicator)
47	     - Lag features from the load itself:
48	       `lag_24h`, `lag_168h` (1 week), `lag_8760h` (~1 year, day-of-week
49	       aligned via the 364-day offset if cleaner)
50	     - Rolling-window features: 24 h and 168 h moving averages and stds
51	       of the load, computed *only* on data ≤ each row's timestamp.
52	   For each test-window hour, all required lags must be present in the
53	   data (they are: 8760 h before 2020-01-01 is 2018-12-31 16:00 UTC,
54	   well inside the training period).
55	
56	5. **N-BEATS** — univariate deep MLP-based forecaster via
57	   `darts.models.NBEATSModel`. Use the default
58	   stack configuration; `input_chunk_length=168` (one week of context),
59	   `output_chunk_length=168` (the forecast horizon), at most ~30 epochs
60	   with early stopping on validation MAPE.
61	
62	6. **PatchTST** — univariate transformer forecaster via
63	   `darts.models.TSMixerModel` or `darts.models.PatchTSTModel` if the
64	   installed darts version exposes it; otherwise substitute another
65	   transformer-based univariate model from the darts catalogue and record
66	   the substitution in `transcript.md`. Same input/output chunk lengths
67	   as N-BEATS. At most ~30 epochs with early stopping.
68	
69	## Allowed inputs
70	
71	- The load series itself (`DE_load_actual_entsoe_transparency`).
72	- Features derived from the `utc_timestamp` column without consulting any
73	  external dataset: `hour`, `day_of_week`, `month`, `is_weekend`,
74	  `is_public_holiday_de` (German federal holidays via the `holidays`
75	  package — knowable a priori, not exogenous data).
76	- Lag features and rolling-window features computed from the load itself.
77	
78	## Forbidden inputs
79	
80	- **External data**: temperature, weather, gas prices, day-ahead market
81	  prices, EUA carbon prices, anything not in `opsd_de_load.csv`.
82	- If you find yourself wanting to bring in such data, stop and record why
83	  in `transcript.md`. The univariate constraint is deliberate: this study
84	  isolates the temporal-structure component of forecast skill, not the
85	  weather-dependence component.
86	
87	## Splits
88	
89	- **Train (initial fit and hyperparameter sweeps):**
90	  2015-01-01 00:00 to 2019-09-30 23:00 (≈4.75 years, ~41,500 rows).
91	- **Validation (hyperparameter / model-order selection):**
92	  2019-10-01 00:00 to 2019-12-31 23:00 (~2,200 rows).
93	- **Test (held out, never touched during fitting or selection):**
94	  2020-01-01 00:00 to 2020-01-07 23:00 (168 hours).
95	
96	Workflow per model:
97	1. Fit on Train.
98	2. Select hyperparameters by evaluating on Validation.
99	3. Refit the chosen configuration on **Train + Validation** combined
100	   (2015-01-01 to 2019-12-31). This is standard practice — final model
101	   uses all data prior to the test window.
102	4. Forecast the 168 test hours.
103	5. Score against the held-out test observations.
104	
105	The naive baseline does not need step 2 (no hyperparameters); it is fit
106	implicitly on whatever lags it needs.
107	
108	## Metrics
109	
110	Compute and report for **every model** on the test window:
111	
112	- **MAPE** — mean absolute percentage error (primary metric).
113	- **RMSE** — root mean square error in MW.
114	- **MAE** — mean absolute error in MW.
115	- **Holiday-vs-working-day MAPE breakdown**: MAPE restricted to Jan 1
116	  (Wednesday, German public holiday) and MAPE on Jan 2–7 separately.
117	  This is where models that don't model holidays will be exposed.
118	
119	For the **winning model** (lowest test MAPE):
120	
121	- **80% and 95% prediction-interval coverage** — fraction of actuals
122	  inside each interval. Report both nominal and actual coverage.
123	- **Pinball loss** at quantiles 0.1, 0.5, 0.9.
124	
125	Probabilistic forecasts are required for SARIMA, Prophet, N-BEATS, and
126	PatchTST (their libraries support sampling or analytic intervals).
127	LightGBM can use `LGBMRegressor` with quantile objective at the 0.1, 0.5,
128	0.9 quantiles (three fits) to produce intervals. The naive baseline
129	does not produce intervals.
130	
131	## Output structure
132	
133	Write into the current working directory only:
134	
135	```
136	code/
137	    common.py         — data loading, evaluation utilities, figure style
138	    naive.py
139	    sarima.py
140	    prophet.py
141	    lightgbm_features.py
142	    nbeats.py
143	    patchtst.py
144	    forecast.py       — orchestrator: runs all six, writes outputs
145	figures/
146	    01_overview.png
147	    02_forecast_comparison.png
148	    03_metric_comparison.png
149	    04_per_day_mape.png
150	    05_winner_with_intervals.png
151	    06_residuals.png
152	    07_feature_importance.png   (only if LightGBM wins or is plotted anyway)
153	    08_decomposition.png        (only if Prophet is the winner)
154	metrics.json
155	metrics.csv
156	transcript.md
157	```
158	
159	## Figures
160	
161	All figures: **300 dpi, sans-serif (matplotlib default), clear axis labels
162	with units in parentheses, non-overlapping legends, consistent `tab10` or
163	`Set2` qualitative palette across figures so each model has the same colour
164	in every plot.** Time-series figures: 11 × 6 in. Square comparisons: 6 × 6 in.
165	
166	1. **`01_overview.png`** — the full load series 2015-01-01 → 2020-09-30 in
167	   light grey, with the 168-hour test window highlighted in red. One panel,
168	   gives the reader spatial context.
169	
170	2. **`02_forecast_comparison.png`** — small multiples, 2 × 3 grid (one
171	   subplot per model). Each subplot shows the test-week observed values
172	   in black and that model's point forecast in its assigned colour. Same
173	   y-axis range across all six panels. Title per subplot: model name +
174	   its MAPE. Saves eye-strain vs overlaying six lines.
175	
176	3. **`03_metric_comparison.png`** — bar chart of MAPE, RMSE, MAE per model
177	   (three grouped bars per model, six models). Sort by MAPE ascending. Show
178	   the numeric value above each bar.
179	
180	4. **`04_per_day_mape.png`** — heatmap or grouped bars of per-day MAPE
181	   (7 days × 6 models). This is where the holiday weakness becomes visible:
182	   most models should have a tall bar on Jan 1.
183	
184	5. **`05_winner_with_intervals.png`** — winning model's forecast on the
185	   test week with 80% (lighter band) and 95% (lighter still) prediction
186	   intervals; observed in black; point forecast in the winner's colour.
187	   Caption: model name + test MAPE + actual 80% / 95% coverage rates.
188	
189	6. **`06_residuals.png`** — winning model's residuals on the test window,
190	   broken down by hour-of-day (left subplot, box plot or violin) and
191	   day-of-week-of-week-in-test (right subplot). Tells the reader where the
192	   winner systematically over- or under-predicts.
193	
194	7. **`07_feature_importance.png`** *(produce if LightGBM is in the top 2,
195	   not just if it wins)* — `LGBMRegressor` feature importances (gain),
196	   sorted descending.
197	
198	8. **`08_decomposition.png`** *(produce if Prophet is in the top 2)* —
199	   trend, weekly, yearly components from the fitted Prophet model.
200	
201	## `metrics.json` schema
202	
203	```json
204	{
205	  "test_start": "2020-01-01",
206	  "test_end":   "2020-01-07",
207	  "n_test_observations": 168,
208	  "models": [
209	    {
210	      "name": "<naive|sarima|prophet|lightgbm|nbeats|patchtst>",
211	      "mape_test_pct": 0.0,
212	      "rmse_test_mw":  0.0,
213	      "mae_test_mw":   0.0,
214	      "mape_jan1_pct": 0.0,
215	      "mape_jan2_to_jan7_pct": 0.0,
216	      "runtime_seconds": 0.0,
217	      "hyperparameters": {}
218	    }
219	  ],
220	  "winner": "<model name>",
221	  "winner_coverage_80pct": 0.0,
222	  "winner_coverage_95pct": 0.0,
223	  "winner_pinball_loss_q10": 0.0,
224	  "winner_pinball_loss_q50": 0.0,
225	  "winner_pinball_loss_q90": 0.0,
226	  "total_runtime_seconds": 0.0
227	}
228	```
229	
230	`metrics.csv` is the same content flattened into rows, one row per model.
231	
232	## `transcript.md`
233	
234	Short methods-section-style write-up, in this order:
235	
236	1. **Data** — one paragraph: source, coverage, the 50,400 rows, why no
237	   imputation was needed.
238	2. **Why these six models** — one paragraph: the complexity gradient and
239	   what each model is supposed to bring.
240	3. **Validation strategy** — one paragraph: train / val / test sizes,
241	   refit-on-train+val rationale.
242	4. **Results table** — markdown table with MAPE / RMSE / MAE per model
243	   plus the holiday-vs-working-day breakdown. Sort by MAPE ascending.
244	5. **Discussion** — 200-400 words. Which model won and why. Where each
245	   model failed (especially on the Jan 1 holiday). Whether the rank
246	   ordering is what theory would predict. Any caveats.
247	6. **Recommendation** — one paragraph: if you had to put exactly one of
248	   these into a JRC production short-term load forecasting pipeline,
249	   which would you pick and what additional work would you do first?
250	7. **Reproducibility note** — random seeds used, total wall-clock
251	   runtime, hardware (`uname -a` output).
252	
253	# DO NOT
254	
255	- Do not use the test window (2020-01-01 to 2020-01-07) for any model
256	  fitting, hyperparameter selection, or model-class choice. The test
257	  window is reserved for the final evaluation only.
258	- During initial fitting and hyperparameter sweeps, do not use data after
259	  2019-09-30 23:00. The validation window (2019-10-01 to 2019-12-31) is
260	  only for scoring candidate hyperparameter / model-order choices. After
261	  selection is finalised, refitting on Train + Validation combined is
262	  **required**, not optional.
263	- Do not pull in external data: temperature, weather, gas prices, market
264	  prices, anything not in `opsd_de_load.csv`. Features derived from the

268	- Do not silently drop or impute missing hours. The data has been

271	- Do not skip the validation step for any model with hyperparameters.
272	- Do not edit any file under `prompts/` or any file under `runs/` outside
273	  this directory.
274	- Do not produce a figure that lacks units, axis labels, a title, or a
275	  consistent colour mapping with the other figures.
276	- Do not omit any required output: all six figures (plus the two optional

279	- Do not install additional Python packages. Everything you need

19	  segment of a stacked bar, and every adjacent (touching) bar, the same width. Keep it
20	  one consistent width across a stack; neighbors one step apart read distinct because of
21	  the gap, not a stroke drawn around them.

25	  are easy to under-size for hover).
26

28	mechanism; a stroke adds data-weight ink that isn't data.

33	channel; never make the reader rely on color-matching alone. Direct labels then ride

35	one color, so the chart's title or subtitle already says what is plotted. A box with

41	  Direct labels work *because* they are sparing - flood the chart and they stop working.

43	- **A label that won't fit doesn't get clipped - measure first.** Only place a label

46	  outside the bar end (or to the tooltip if there's no room outside either); for an

  the story is about; let the axis, the legend, and the tooltip/table carry the rest.

- **A label that won't fit doesn't get clipped - measure first.** Only place a label

from __future__ import annotations

import sys
import types
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import pytest

PACKAGE = types.ModuleType("study")
PACKAGE.__path__ = [str(Path(__file__).resolve().parent)]
sys.modules.setdefault("study", PACKAGE)

from study.common import load_data, mape, quantile_diagnostics, score, validation_blocks
from study.lightgbm_features import FEATURES, feature_frame, recursive_forecast


def test_verified_data_and_split_contract() -> None:
    data = load_data()
    assert len(data) == 50400
    assert len(data.loc[:"2019-09-30 23:00"]) == 41616
    assert len(data.loc["2019-10-01":"2019-12-31 23:00"]) == 2208
    assert len(data.loc["2020-01-01":"2020-01-07 23:00"]) == 168
    assert data.index[0].tzinfo is not None


def test_every_validation_hour_scored_once() -> None:
    data = load_data().loc[:"2019-12-31 23:00"]
    blocks = list(validation_blocks(data))
    assert [len(target) for _, target in blocks] == [168] * 13 + [24]
    index = pd.DatetimeIndex([])
    for history, target in blocks:
        assert history.index[-1] + pd.Timedelta(hours=1) == target.index[0]
        index = index.append(target.index)
    assert index.equals(data.loc["2019-10-01":].index)
    assert index.is_unique


def test_metric_formulas_and_units() -> None:
    actual = np.array([100.0, 200.0])
    pred = np.array([90.0, 240.0])
    assert mape(actual, pred) == pytest.approx(15.0)
    result = score(actual, pred)
    assert result["mae_test_mw"] == pytest.approx(25.0)
    assert result["rmse_test_mw"] == pytest.approx(np.sqrt(850.0))
    q = np.tile([80.0, 90.0, 100.0, 110.0, 120.0], (2, 1))
    diagnostics = quantile_diagnostics(np.array([100.0, 115.0]), q)
    assert diagnostics["winner_coverage_80pct"] == 0.5
    assert diagnostics["winner_coverage_95pct"] == 1.0
    assert diagnostics["winner_pinball_loss_q50"] == 3.75


def test_rolling_features_exclude_current_and_future_targets() -> None:
    index = pd.date_range("2017-01-01", periods=9000, freq="h", tz="UTC")
    series = pd.Series(np.arange(9000, dtype=float) + 1000, index=index)
    first = feature_frame(series)
    changed = series.copy()
    changed.iloc[8800:] = -999999.0
    second = feature_frame(changed)
    np.testing.assert_array_equal(first.iloc[8800].values, second.iloc[8800].values)
    assert first.iloc[8800]["rolling_mean_24h"] == series.iloc[8776:8800].mean()
    assert first.iloc[8800]["lag_8760h"] == series.iloc[40]
    assert first.iloc[8800]["rolling_std_168h"] == pytest.approx(series.iloc[8632:8800].std(ddof=0))


class Lag24Predictor:
    def predict(self, matrix: np.ndarray, **kwargs: object) -> np.ndarray:
        return matrix[:, FEATURES.index("lag_24h")] + 1.0


def test_recursive_forecast_uses_its_own_unobserved_lags() -> None:
    index = pd.date_range("2017-01-01", periods=9000, freq="h", tz="UTC")
    history = pd.Series(np.arange(9000, dtype=float) + 1000, index=index)
    future = pd.date_range(index[-1] + pd.Timedelta(hours=1), periods=168, freq="h")
    prediction = recursive_forecast({0.5: Lag24Predictor()}, history, future)
    np.testing.assert_array_equal(prediction[:24, 0], history.iloc[-24:].values + 1.0)
    np.testing.assert_array_equal(prediction[24:48, 0], prediction[:24, 0] + 1.0)
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="immediately"):
        recursive_forecast({0.5: Lag24Predictor()}, history, future + pd.Timedelta(hours=1))

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from lightgbm import LGBMRegressor

from .common import QUANTILES, SEED, TEST_INDEX, TRAIN_END, ForecastResult, mape, validation_blocks

FEATURES = [
    "hour", "day_of_week", "month", "is_weekend", "is_public_holiday_de",
    "lag_24h", "lag_168h", "lag_8760h", "rolling_mean_24h", "rolling_std_24h",
    "rolling_mean_168h", "rolling_std_168h",
]
HOLIDAYS = holidays.Germany(years=range(2015, 2021))
CANDIDATES = [{"num_leaves": 15, "n_estimators": 250}, {"num_leaves": 31, "n_estimators": 400}]


def calendar_features(index: pd.DatetimeIndex) -> np.ndarray:
    return np.column_stack([
        index.hour, index.dayofweek, index.month, (index.dayofweek >= 5).astype(int),
        [int(timestamp.date() in HOLIDAYS) for timestamp in index],
    ]).astype(float)


def feature_frame(series: pd.Series) -> pd.DataFrame:
    frame = pd.DataFrame(calendar_features(series.index), index=series.index, columns=FEATURES[:5])
    for lag in [24, 168, 8760]:
        frame[f"lag_{lag}h"] = series.shift(lag)
    past = series.shift(1)
    for window in [24, 168]:
        frame[f"rolling_mean_{window}h"] = past.rolling(window).mean()
        frame[f"rolling_std_{window}h"] = past.rolling(window).std(ddof=0)
    return frame[FEATURES]


def recursive_forecast(models: dict[float, Any], history: pd.Series, future: pd.DatetimeIndex) -> np.ndarray:
    if future[0] != history.index[-1] + pd.Timedelta(hours=1):
        raise ValueError("Forecast must start immediately after observed history")
    if len(history) < 8760:
        raise ValueError("Insufficient annual lag history")
    if not future.equals(pd.date_range(future[0], periods=len(future), freq="h")):
        raise ValueError("Forecast timestamps must be hourly and contiguous")
    levels = sorted(models)
    median_column = levels.index(0.5)
    values = np.empty(len(history) + len(future), dtype=float)
    values[:len(history)] = history.to_numpy()
    calendar = calendar_features(future)
    output = np.empty((len(future), len(models)))
    for step in range(len(future)):
        position = len(history) + step
        last24, last168 = values[position-24:position], values[position-168:position]
        row = np.concatenate([calendar[step], [
            values[position-24], values[position-168], values[position-8760],
            last24.mean(), last24.std(ddof=0), last168.mean(), last168.std(ddof=0),
        ]]).reshape(1, -1)
        predictions = [float(models[level].predict(row)[0]) for level in levels]
        output[step] = np.sort(predictions)
        # Only the predicted median enters any later hour's features.
        values[position] = output[step, median_column]
    return output


def fit_models(series: pd.Series, config: dict[str, int], levels: list[float]) -> dict[float, Any]:
    features = feature_frame(series)
    complete = features.notna().all(axis=1)
    x = features.loc[complete].to_numpy()
    y = series.loc[complete].to_numpy()
    models = {}
    for level in levels:
        model = LGBMRegressor(
            objective="quantile", alpha=level, learning_rate=0.05,
            min_child_samples=40, reg_lambda=1.0, verbosity=-1,
            random_state=SEED, n_jobs=4, deterministic=True, force_col_wise=True,
            **config,
        )
        model.fit(x, y)
        models[level] = model.booster_
    return models


def run(pretest: pd.Series) -> ForecastResult:
    start = perf_counter()
    train = pretest.loc[:TRAIN_END]
    records = []
    for config in CANDIDATES:
        models = fit_models(train, config, [0.5])
        actuals, predictions = [], []
        for history, target in validation_blocks(pretest):
            predictions.extend(recursive_forecast(models, history, target.index)[:, 0])
            actuals.extend(target.values)
        value = mape(np.array(actuals), np.array(predictions))
        records.append({"configuration": config, "mape_validation_pct": value})
        print(f"lightgbm validation {config}: {value:.4f}%", flush=True)
    selected = min(records, key=lambda record: record["mape_validation_pct"])["configuration"]
    final_models = fit_models(pretest, selected, QUANTILES)
    quantiles = recursive_forecast(final_models, pretest, TEST_INDEX)
    importance = final_models[0.5].feature_importance(importance_type="gain")
    return ForecastResult(
        name="lightgbm", point=quantiles[:, 2], quantiles=quantiles,
        runtime_seconds=perf_counter() - start,
        hyperparameters={**selected, "learning_rate": 0.05, "min_child_samples": 40,
                         "reg_lambda": 1.0, "objective": "quantile", "quantiles": QUANTILES,
                         "lag_hours": [24, 168, 8760], "rolling_ddof": 0, "seed": SEED,
                         "forecast_strategy": "recursive median path, sorted marginal quantiles"},
        validation=records,
        diagnostics={"gain_importance": dict(zip(FEATURES, importance.tolist())),
                     "training_rows_lost_to_lag_warmup": 8760,
                     "interval_caveat": "One-step quantiles conditioned on recursive median features; lag uncertainty is not propagated."},
    )

from __future__ import annotations

import warnings
from time import perf_counter
from typing import Any

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy.stats import norm
from statsmodels.tsa.statespace.sarimax import SARIMAX

from .common import QUANTILES, TEST_INDEX, TRAIN_END, ForecastResult, mape, validation_blocks

CANDIDATES = [(1, 0, 0), (2, 0, 0)]
SEASONAL_ORDER = (1, 1, 0, 24)


def weekly_fourier(index: pd.DatetimeIndex) -> np.ndarray:
    hours = (index - pd.Timestamp("2015-01-01", tz="UTC")).total_seconds().to_numpy() / 3600.0
    return np.column_stack([
        function(2.0 * np.pi * harmonic * hours / 168.0)
        for harmonic in [1, 2, 3]
        for function in [np.sin, np.cos]
    ])


def fit(series: pd.Series, order: tuple[int, int, int], scale: float) -> tuple[Any, list[str]]:
    with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
        warnings.simplefilter("always")
        model = SARIMAX(
            series.to_numpy() / scale, exog=weekly_fourier(series.index),
            order=order, seasonal_order=SEASONAL_ORDER,
            enforce_stationarity=False, enforce_invertibility=False,
            concentrate_scale=True,
        )
        result = model.fit(disp=False, maxiter=60, low_memory=True)
    messages = sorted({str(warning.message) for warning in caught})
    return result, messages


def run(pretest: pd.Series) -> ForecastResult:
    start = perf_counter()
    train = pretest.loc[:TRAIN_END]
    scale = float(train.mean())
    records = []
    for order in CANDIDATES:
        fitted, messages = fit(train, order, scale)
        state = fitted
        predictions, actuals = [], []
        for _, target in validation_blocks(pretest):
            predicted = state.get_forecast(len(target), exog=weekly_fourier(target.index))
            predictions.extend(np.asarray(predicted.predicted_mean) * scale)
            actuals.extend(target.values)
            # Filtering advances the origin with known history; coefficients stay frozen.
            state = state.extend(target.to_numpy() / scale, exog=weekly_fourier(target.index))
        value = mape(np.array(actuals), np.array(predictions))
        records.append({"order": list(order), "mape_validation_pct": value,
                        "converged": bool(fitted.mle_retvals.get("converged", False)),
                        "warnings": messages, "iterations": int(fitted.mle_retvals.get("iterations", 0))})
        print(f"sarima validation {order}: {value:.4f}% converged={records[-1]['converged']}", flush=True)
    eligible = [record for record in records if record["converged"]]
    if not eligible:
        raise RuntimeError("No SARIMA candidate converged; do not report an unverified fit")
    selected = tuple(min(eligible, key=lambda record: record["mape_validation_pct"])["order"])
    final_scale = float(pretest.mean())
    final, messages = fit(pretest, selected, final_scale)
    if not final.mle_retvals.get("converged", False):
        raise RuntimeError("Final SARIMA refit failed to converge")
    forecast = final.get_forecast(168, exog=weekly_fourier(TEST_INDEX))
    point = np.asarray(forecast.predicted_mean) * final_scale
    sigma = np.asarray(forecast.se_mean) * final_scale
    quantiles = point[:, None] + sigma[:, None] * norm.ppf(QUANTILES)[None, :]
    return ForecastResult(
        name="sarima", point=point, quantiles=quantiles, runtime_seconds=perf_counter() - start,
        hyperparameters={"order": list(selected), "seasonal_order": list(SEASONAL_ORDER),
                         "weekly_fourier_harmonics": 3, "maxiter": 60,
                         "enforce_stationarity": False, "enforce_invertibility": False,
                         "concentrate_scale": True, "intervals": "Gaussian state-space forecast errors, fixed estimated parameters"},
        validation=records,
        diagnostics={"final_converged": True, "final_warnings": messages,
                     "final_iterations": int(final.mle_retvals.get("iterations", 0))},
    )

content.thinking:
I'm realizing that stride-168 severely under-samples the data, giving only ~245 windows per epoch and just ~7,400 gradient samples across 30 epochs for a 2.3M parameter model. Switching to stride 24 gives roughly 1,720 samples per epoch at a still-fast 1.4-6s per epoch, and even stride 1 with ~41,280 samples only takes about 10s total.

Then I catch a more serious problem: stride 168 aligns every training window to the exact same weekday phase. Since training ends Monday 23:00, every window's input starts Tuesday 00:00, but the test origin is Wednesday and validation origin is Tuesday - so there's a phase mismatch between what the model learned and what it's being tested on. Since N-BEATS has no calendar covariates, it has no way to distinguish this shift, and any weekday structure it learned implicitly would be misaligned at test time.

I'd recommend stride 24 as a minimum, or even stride 1 given the tractable runtimes involved. On the early stopping question, I realize Darts' built-in mechanism tracks val_loss (quantile loss on scaled data) rather than MAPE, so achieving true early stopping on rolling-origin MAPE requires a manual epoch-by-epoch loop, and I need to check how Darts handles continued training when calling fit repeatedly on a model with epochs already trained.

So that means picking an epoch count and refitting from scratch trains a genuinely different trajectory than the validated one. A more honest approach would be a single fit run with a callback that computes rolling validation MAPE at each epoch end directly via a forward pass on manually built validation windows, then stops early based on that signal instead of relying on separate refit calls.

For the "validation observations providing context" question: NBEATS/Transformer naturally use the 168h window preceding each forecast origin as input, so later validation weeks get earlier validation data as context automatically -- that's fine since it's just inference context, not fitting, and training-only scaling still holds. SARIMAX can incorporate validation context legitimately by running the Kalman filter forward with fixed parameters via apply/extend without refitting. Prophet, however, has no internal state to carry validation context forward.

Prophet's forecasts across the validation set are essentially a long extrapolation from the training fit alone, stretching up to 13 weeks ahead, while it later gets refit on train+val for the 1-week-ahead test forecast -- this creates a fairness asymmetry rather than leakage, since Prophet's validation MAPE is disproportionately shaped by long-horizon trend extrapolation and thus biases the changepoint prior selection toward the more conservative option. I'm weighing whether this asymmetry is acceptable as long as it's disclosed, versus whether refitting Prophet per origin using only data up to that point would better preserve fairness without violating the training-only fitting rule.

For LightGBM and SARIMAX, using lagged and rolling features or Kalman-filtered context from prior validation observations seems properly handled -- these methods use past validation data as legitimate context without retraining parameters. I'm also confirming the validation scoring window spans exactly 2,208 hours (13 full weeks plus a final 24-hour remainder), and now turning to how SARIMAX's weekly Fourier regressors interact with the seasonal differencing at lag 24 -- since seasonal differencing at D=1 doesn't automatically apply to exogenous regressors in the state-space formulation, the interaction between the ARIMA component and the exogenous terms depends on how differencing is implemented.

Working through the harmonic structure, I realize the k=7 harmonic (24-hour period) gets completely annihilated by the 24-hour seasonal difference, creating a singular exogenous matrix, so I need to restrict Fourier harmonics to k=1 through 6 and verify full rank after differencing. The weekly Fourier terms will still be attenuated but not zeroed for these harmonics, which is acceptable, though I note this approach only crudely captures the weekend-specific daily shape difference — not a blocker, just a limitation to flag alongside the New Year's Day holiday consideration.
